summaryBox.title: Axiomatic Core
summaryBox.takeaway: Unrestricted comprehension leads to Russell's Paradox; ZFC set theory restricts set formation to well-defined predicates over existing domains.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
ELEMENTHOOD AND MEMBERSHIP
                                     │
         ┌───────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                       ▼
   STATEMENT: x ∈ A                                        STATEMENT: x ∉ A
   x is an element of set A                                x is NOT an element of set A
   (Truth Value = TRUE)                                    (Truth Value = FALSE)
conceptBreakdown.content:
A **Set** is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements or members. The phrase *well-defined* signifies that for any given object $x$ and any set $A$, there is a fundamental, non-ambiguous truth value to the statement $x \in A$ or $x \notin A$.

### Axiomatic Note (Naive vs. Rigorous Set Theory)
In naive set theory, unrestricted comprehension permits the formation of sets like $R = \{x \mid x \notin x\}$. This leads directly to **Russell’s Paradox** ($R \in R \iff R \notin R$). To avoid such antinomies, modern mathematics operates within Zermelo-Fraenkel Set Theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC), where sets are constructed from primitive elements under strict formation axioms.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.1 Methods of Representing Sets
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.1 Methods of Representing Sets
conceptBreakdown.content:
1. **Roster or Tabular Form**: All elements are listed explicitly within curly braces, separated by commas. The order of elements is irrelevant, and elements are non-repeating ($I = \{1, 2, 3\} \equiv \{3, 1, 2\}$).
2. **Set-Builder or Rule Form**: A set is specified by a characteristic predicate $P(x)$ that uniquely identifies its members:
$$A = \{x \mid P(x)\} \quad \text{or} \quad A = \{x \in S \mid P(x)\}$$
Read as: "The set of all $x$ in $S$ such that $P(x)$ is true."
